Report 28: a weekly-target-only model — monthly, every-other-week, multiple-times-per-day and specific-weekday scheduling requested by 15 (1.83%), one explicitly blocking a purchase: 'I can't see myself purchasing without being able to make these distinctions'. Report 29: weekday checkboxes only — x times per week without naming days ('practice golf 3 times a week but it doesn't matter on which days'), every other week ('My off days Fri, Sat, Sun every other week… its frustrating' — the only feature-driven 1★), monthly and custom intervals (14, 3.83%) — the one structural gap persisting across all five half-years. Report 30: non-daily scheduling (days of week, x per week, weekly, monthly) is the only feature gap with multi-market evidence — 4 storefronts, 4 languages — and the only build item the report supports. Report 31: 'N times per period' with no fixed days is praised by 81 (a monthly view prevents 'feel bad' spirals); removing monthly and yearly frequencies (Dec 2022 – Jan 2023) drew 58 requests still arriving in 2026 ('This was the ONE reason I used to love this app'; contact lenses monthly, weight loss yearly; 'call friend once a month or take a vacation three times a year'; deep-clean the oven monthly). Report 33: 'N times a week' and every-N-days frequency are named differentiators (flexible scheduling praised 79, mean 4.80); 'N per week' was removed in Habitify X and restored; monthly nth-weekday and end dates are still requested (82; haircut, bills on the 15th, can't end a 30-day challenge). Report 34: x-days-per-week added on request (Apr 2019), flexible frequency praised by 13 (mean 4.92); every-other-day and monthly targets still requested (7). Report 36: flexible schedules (every N days, N×/week or month) requested by 7 in E1–E3 and not since Dec 2024 (probably addressed); habits shown on unscheduled days (3, all 4–5★). Report 41: 'X times per week, any days' / 'every N days' (13) and seeing which day a weekly habit was done (9) — one request asked twice, every year 2021–2026, 8 of 13 at 4★: 'I would like the option of doing something 3 times a week, not necessarily on the same day'; the app models which-days and how-many-times as alternatives. Report 42: setting which days, dates and repetition is Premium ('task repetition is paid-plan only', JP 1★); 'Tue & Thu' and shifting a habit to another day requested. Report 43: scheduling flexibility is the longest-running unaddressed request (29, 4.55%, mean 3.38; Jan 2017 → Jan 2025) — intervals beyond one month ('Wish I'd known that before I paid for it'), Nth weekday ('1st Tuesday of each month'), 'X times per week' without fixed days, every other week, a due date rolling from last completion; a redesign regression made 'every 2/3 weeks' habits show every week.

title: Mac / desktop / web app
statement: Strongest 3★ driver; users volunteer to pay extra for it. Report 23: the Mac app was a separate purchase in 2020–21, then included in the universal purchase from late 2021 (≥8 reviews, a classifier miss at 1); one unverified report of the Mac app creating millions of files and locking the user out. Report 25: a Mac app is part of the included platform surface (8 mentions, mean 4.00). Report 27: a macOS app requested once, 5★. Report 31: iPad / Mac / landscape / web / Android wanted by 98 (1.89%, mean 3.49), peaking in the 4★ band (7.5%) and in E1 (5.3%), falling to ~1% after 2021 as those users left. Report 33: a Mac app (sold separately in 2018), a menu-bar mini app, web, Android and Windows exist; the Mac app could not sign in or sync through 2021–22 (Mac/web 18.5% of 2022, Russia 10.1%) until macOS 13.0.1. Report 34: no iPad / Mac / web app (8) — 'The only reason i'm going with a competitor … is because I don't always want to use my phone'; 'I'd even pay for separate versions as long as they synced'. Report 43: a macOS / desktop app requested by 3 (mean 4.67); the listing claims Mac (M1+) — possibly discoverability.

title: Grouping / folders / categories / tags
statement: #2 feature request in report 1; the highest-mean request in report 3 (zero 1–2★, power users tracking 20–100 counters); named in report 8's only subscription-price statement. Report 20: categories/folders (58) and a compact row option (26) co-occur — both are what happens when a power user exceeds ~8 habits. Report 23: extra capacity is wanted for time-of-day pages (morning / work / evening / bedtime) and life-domain segmentation (health / work / relationships / creative). Report 25: groups and sub-groups are a praised paid feature (customisation 65, mean 4.49); group creation reported locked on free. Report 26: per-habit gardens or categories requested (18). Report 27: tags exist but existing tags cannot be selected and duplicates don't group — two storefronts, two months apart, same bug, both cost stars. Report 31: groups/categories (added Mar 2018) were paid and valued by buyers; forced daily/weekly grouping and order resets in v3.0 (22) drew complaints. Report 33: areas / folders (Dec 2019) are free and mixed (31). Report 41: lists / tags with per-list rings and widget filtering (2022).

title: Shortcuts / Siri / URL scheme / API
statement: Power users who evangelise. Report 23: Siri Shortcuts, URL actions and NFC triggers are a power-user favourite (72, 0.99%, mean 3.94). Report 25: Siri Shortcuts exist; a Mac app and formerly Vision Pro; Shortcuts gaps 1. Report 31: Siri Shortcuts were removed in the Mar 2022 rebuild and automations broke (14). Report 33: x-callback / Shortcuts, Zapier / IFTTT, a public API, calendar sync and NFC habits serve power users (47, rising to 2.5% of E5; API 'unbeatable'; 'Pairs nicely with agentic workflows'); Siri Shortcuts broke in Habitify X. Report 41: Siri Shortcuts with near-full app control praised by 36 ('I was able to automate 80% of habits tracking'); public API / Zapier / IFTTT requested by 5. Report 43: Siri / Shortcuts praised by 5 (all US); one asks for Shortcuts integration.

title: Cumulative totals and total-days counter
statement: '47 hours read this year'; total days instead of consecutive to reduce streak anxiety.

title: Flexible units / partial progress
statement: Drag to 60% instead of a binary tick — a named reason for choosing over competitors. Report 23: 77 reviews (1.06%) in seven languages ask to record effort beyond the goal or short of it — over-achievement is discarded ('goal 30 minutes, read 90, it stops at 30') and partial progress renders as failure ('6 of 8 glasses shows an ✗'); the two most-upvoted reviews in the 7,270-review corpus (313 and 126 votes) are this request; 'do 30 push-ups' breaks on a 25 day where 'push-ups per day' would record 25 and preserve momentum. Ship floor-without-ceiling goals and a partial-progress calendar state without changing the streak rule. Report 25: measurement units — count, minutes, distance, custom steps — and track-only habits with no goal number. Report 29: quantity/unit tracking (steps, litres, reps; one proposes a slider) requested by 4 — only as an optional habit type outside the default flow. Report 31: unit tracking with custom increments (dollar amounts for business referrals) is praised; a custom-count input bug added an extra unit ('I type in 50 pages … it counts 55', 16). Report 33: goals with units and multiple check-ins per day shipped in Aug 2020; custom units (kg, kcal, metric) and icons still requested (56). Report 34: quantity / partial completion requested by 11 — 'I Drank 80oz … I wanna be able to track that'; '8 of 10 glasses counts as progress'. Report 36: multiple completions per day / quantity targets (water in ounces) requested by 5. Report 43: multiple completions per day with 0/2, 0/4 counters (water, reps) exist free and are a purchase trigger ('the 0/2, 0/4 etc feature that visually shows you how far behind you are… it made me buy it'); praised by 14 (mean 4.71).

title: Mood tracker
statement: Meaningful praise where shipped; mentions rose after launch (report 1); asked for only by 5★ users (report 8); an automatic mood prompt is a memory aid and moving it behind a button destroyed users' mood datasets (report 10). Report 24: a daily mood check-in exists inside the routine app. Report 25: a Russian lifetime buyer with ADHD proposes a mood/energy tracker so the statistics screen can answer why a habit failed. Report 28: a mood tracker with limited free moods (paid moods 10 complaints, mean 3.90; mood entry mandatory on open 2); journal/mood used by 38 (4.63%, mean 4.29). Report 33: a mood log (Aug 2021) with multiple moods per day as Premium — 14 mentions, mixed. Report 41: mood tracking added via Apple Health (Sep 2024, 'I'm very happy to see mood tracking added'); 5 wanted it inside the app's own history.

title: One-off to-dos alongside habits
statement: Emerging request. Report 18: routines and one-off to-dos interleaved in one time-ordered list was a named purchase trigger and 'MyRoutine's one advantage' over to-do apps; to-do parity (carry-over, subtasks, tags, priority, undated, recurring) was requested ~30 times. Report 25: one-off, non-repeating tasks in a separate list or tab requested by 10 (7 of them 4★) alongside the time-of-day request. Report 28: a to-do checklist exists separately from habits and users want it to earn carrots (9, mean 4.44 — 'the more irksome and time consuming tasks that you procrastinate on'). Report 31: one-off tasks / today-only items requested by 28 (mean 2.86). Report 33: one-off tasks requested by 10.

title: Android version
statement: Requested; cross-platform continuity matters to switchers. Report 26: Android asked about repeatedly (CN, FR, SE). Report 31: Android and web appear in the 98 platform requests.

title: Points / rewards / wish list
statement: Weak request; one proposes a cash-stake mode.

title: Custom time-of-day segments
statement: Beyond morning/afternoon/evening — shift workers. Report 23: one page per time of day — morning, work, evening, bedtime — is the top reason people ask for more capacity. Report 33: time-of-day sections (morning / afternoon / evening / anytime) are a named differentiator — 'no other app does as well'; 'the best thing about Habitify' — and paired with flexible frequency form 'a winning core'; a hidden time-of-day filter also produced false bug reports.

title: Never run incentivised / review-for-premium campaigns
statement: Bought rank and a fake average, 0.86% purchase signal, reputational backlash, unreadable data. Report 26: a review-for-cosmetic-unlock reward produced reviewers who volunteer they have not used the app; the ≤25-char 5★ tier doubled to ~35% of the corpus. Report 33: review solicitation — a founder-named 5★ burst (12 Oct – 1 Nov 2018: 110 reviews at mean 4.64 vs 3.30 before), 'a strange email … asking for a rating', a free-lifetime link after reviewing, contests awarding Premium, and a CEO asking for 5★ — 'Who the hell is peter?'; the burst left no durable effect and the report's last cheapest win is to stop it. Report 34: a free-lifetime giveaway (~29 Jun 2023) produced 27 short, mostly 5★ reviews in three days (55.6% ≤ 25 characters) and moved the mean by ~0.01. Report 42: six US 5★ reviews in three days (Aug 2020) with 13–30 helpful votes each and nonsense titles ('Hgfgg', 'Bdbdbd'), and eleven of Canada's twelve reviews 5★ generic praise in 13 days (May 2021) — 17 reviews (8.25%) that inflate the mean from 2.968 to 3.136 and leave Canada unmeasurable. Report 43: a launch-week burst of 13 seeded 5★ reviews inside 24 minutes moved a ten-year corpus by 0.02.

title: Never gate or delete reviews
statement: Users catch it and call it a ToS violation. Report 33: one unverified claim that the developer deleted a review after 5 weeks without support.

title: Don't build AI features on demand grounds
statement: 0.011% demand; users ask for the opposite. Report 23: exactly one review mentions the 'Break It Down' AI feature (May 2026) — and asks for it to be removed. Report 24: an AI chat/coach bubble added ~2025 is an unwanted addition for long-tenure users, and AI-generated art/copy is the worst-rated non-billing theme (64, mean 1.156, 90.6% 1★) — the theme did not exist before 2024. Report 28: zero of 821 reviews request AI features; the only AI mention is a complaint about AI homework-cheating ads served inside the app — 'no evidence of AI demand in this audience'. Report 33: AI 'smart fill' and AI / chatbot support (2025–26) drew mostly negative reviews — 'Stop shoving AI everywhere'. Report 34: across 743 reviews over eight years, no review mentions AI, ChatGPT or an AI feature. Report 36: exactly one review mentions AI — as a substitute after uninstalling over the cap ('doing it with AI daily tasks until I find an alternative'). Report 41: Apple Intelligence habit suggestions shipped (Sep 2025) drew one light positive ('I like the apple AI to help with ideas'), while 'an AI coach' is on the report's do-not-add list.

title: Offer a non-pastel / premium design option
statement: Recurring critique from men and users wanting a premium look. Report 25: native Apple design language reads as premium — ''Apple' design all over it'. Report 26: reviewers convert on beauty within minutes of install ('I bought premium within the first couple minutes of downloading'; 'as soon as I saw the visuals and music I bought premium') — aesthetic is the mechanism, not decoration, and 'It's not just an app it's a piece of art'. Report 29: UI/visual design praised by 45 (12.30%, mean 4.64); a font complaint (1); more colours / custom colours requested (4).

title: Discovery runs through social video, Reddit, therapists (US) and Xiaohongshu / Bilibili (CN)
statement: Plan marketing around where users say they found the app. Report 10: 381 reviews involve a clinician recommending the app; two clinicians publicly withdrew the recommendation over data loss. Report 19 (negative case): paid Instagram/YouTube ads → web quiz → web checkout → a checklist; six reviewers named the channel and the funnel, not the software, generated the corpus. Report 23: therapists and psychologists recommending it to ADHD clients (28, mean 4.50), Atomic Habits and habit literature (14, mean 4.79), podcasts and blogs (Daring Fireball, MacBreak Weekly, Do By Friday, Diary of a CEO; 12, mean ~4.6); Apple editorial / Design Award traffic was the worst channel (17, mean 2.53). Report 24: acquisition runs through Instagram / Facebook / X ads into a web questionnaire; credibility signals (Duke/Stanford framing, Atomic Habits adjacency) and 'the trial produced a result in days' are the conversion stories. Report 25: Instagram / TikTok / Reels ads are a stated acquisition channel for buyers; three arrive via a clinician. Report 31: TikTok / Instagram / YouTube / press named by 117 (mean 1.72), 81 of 98 TikTok mentions in 2022 — the channel that brought the largest audience arrived during a launch crash. Report 34: launched via Reddit (Jul 2018); 6 reviewers (mean 5.00) say they found it via Reddit, social or reviews; early Reddit adopters wrote long, personal reviews to the developer by name. Report 36: an App Store Awards / Apple Design Award feature drove discovery at launch (Jun 2022); a professional coach prescribes the app to clients.

title: Be visibly responsive; fixes bring reviewers back
statement: Users who see their bug fixed return to raise their rating. Report 18: the developer shipped what users asked for — widget, Watch, dark mode, bundles, timer, routine modes — roughly 18–36 months after the request, often breaking something else in the same release; six reviewers raised their rating after a developer reply, and one returning churned subscriber wrote '神✨'. Report 20: users restored in Feb 2021 came back and raised their ratings (23 five-star reviews carry the revocation theme as amended reviews); a 20 Oct 2020 launch failure fixed next day drew praise for the speed. Report 23: 12 edited reviews, several visible upgrades after a developer fix; sync-migration recoveries within weeks; reviewers upgraded on learning a backup path existed. Report 24: a 2018–19 billing crisis was fixed in one month and the mean snapped back from 2.884 to 4.206 for four years; refunds that land turn 1★ into 4★ edits. Report 25: a Turkish localisation request made eight times in Jan–Jun 2026 was answered on 27 Jul 2026 ('Türkçe dil desteği sonundaaa! 🌟') — the clearest shipped-fix-visible-in-reviews event in the corpus. Report 26: a visible 2024 engineering turnaround — crashes 3.37% → 0.13%, the 'music can't be turned off' bug 2.88% → 0.00%, mean 4.339 → 4.675 — with the substantive-only mean rising too; a reviewer thanked the team for adding a calendar; Russian localisation criticised in 2023 was praised by 2025. Report 27: requested features ship on a 6–18 month lag — per-weekday flexibility (Jul 2025 → Mar 2026), reordering (Sept 2024 → Aug 2025), goal end date and archiving (Dec 2025 → on the listing by Sep 2026); the crash was fixed within about four months and the mean recovered to 4.829. Report 28: a 1★ upgraded to 5★ after one support e-mail ('The devs pay attention. 5 stars now'); bugs collapsed from 11.3% (2023) to 0.7% (2025) after a genuine stabilisation. Report 29: the calendar bug fell ~8× between 2025H2 and 2026H1 and the mean rose 4.39 → 4.66; habit editing missing in 2024 was added by May 2025 — but 'a fix ships, and the reviews it caused remain on the store page forever'. Report 30 (counter-evidence): the developer's response to the cap complaint — one more free habit — did not change the rate or the ratings. Report 31: the original solo developer shipped a wished-for feature two days later, replied to a crash e-mail and fixed it 'ASAP', restored a purchase 'within minutes' — support praise 18 (mean 4.78), 11 in E1; after the sale, public developer replies began only in 2024 with split outcomes (restored within days vs a promised refund never issued, 'they sneakily changed their developer response') and support-unresponsive stayed at 20.8% in E5. Report 33: fast fixes after a review earn thanks and rating rises ('thank you for responding right after my review'; a 1★ raised to 4★ after a fix); a public roadmap and feature voting; the Jan 2018 purchase wave fixed in two weeks and the Sep 2025 launch crash in 1–3 days; 'An update improved it' 112 (mean 4.78). Report 34: 52 developer-praise reviews (mean 4.96), 31 naming 'Kevin'; replies turned ratings up ('Updated to 4 stars - thank you devs for the response!'); weekly habits and a reviewer's suggestion built on request; an in-app 'in progress' roadmap list ('this informing and communicative attitude was a huge plus'); the share fell 13.2% (E1) → 5.2% (E5). Report 41: eleven requested capabilities shipped inside the corpus with requesters returning to confirm (notes, Watch, % widget — review edited twice, Shortcuts in the same month, CSV export, vacation mode, heat maps, mood, custom day start 'It was not available at that time, but it is now', Czech / Italian / Traditional Chinese); a support reply 'within hours. Twice' closed a lifetime sale. Report 42: reviewers notice fixes — 'Thanks for the update, it helped remove the lag. I'll bring my subscription back'; 'how much the app has improved in that time! Progress details, results info, charts' — vs 'they just reply the same thing to everyone'. Report 43: at least four verified cases of shipping what reviewers asked — Apple Watch (12 requests, none after it shipped), drag-to-reorder (7 asks, shipped Nov 2025), the timer music fix that turned a 2★ into 5★, and a feature 'added a few days later' (Jan 2026); three of the top four feature gaps have since closed.

title: Cross-sell an app family on brand trust
statement: Under-used monetization asset. Report 23: Streaks is sold in a bundle with Streaks Workout and HealthFace. Report 24 (counter-evidence): a nine-app family (Clarify, Shape, Elixir, Lumière, Lune, Ambiance, Sphere, Mind, Enchant), each its own download and subscription, is experienced as advertising inside a paid product and as a billing trap; Clarify, the ADHD sister app, is named almost only inside billing complaints (mean 1.637). Cross-sell on brand trust works only while the trust and the billing are clean. Report 28: cross-promotion from the sibling app Study Bunny drove launch (31.8% of 2021 reviews, a beta-forgiving cohort with zero 1★) and still drives a tenth of reviews, but fell to 3.8% by 2026 — the app now acquires on its own store presence, so the rating and the ad policy are commercially decisive; users ask for single sign-on and a shared bunny across the family. Report 31 (counter-evidence): the Growth Bundle cross-sell became the only upgrade path and a post-purchase 'gift' upsell that broke entitlements — 36 bundle complaints (mean 2.03). Report 36: a 5-app 'Not Boring' membership — SUITE+ 34 (mean 4.41; 'I purchased the S2 for the weather app, but Habits is really the star for me'; 4 of 34 payers bought for the suite) vs SUITE- 9 (mean 3.22; 'Theoretically it includes 3 other apps, but this is the only good one … the calculator app … lags'): the weakest app in the bundle drags the perceived value of the price.

title: Goodwill conversion — a generous free tier and 'support the devs'
statement: Small, pure-margin, mean 4.69. Report 5: the dominant purchase path was years of free use followed by upgrading to scale it or to say thanks. Report 20: a large share of pre-2021 purchases were donations — 'I'll definitely choose the highest one because this developer deserves the best'; 'I bought the paid function not because I needed it, but as a thank you.' Report 26: 'bought premium right away just to support the developers'; 45 call the free tier generous (mean 4.49). Report 28: 'I've spent money on this app SOLELY to support the developer because I can't thank him enough'; 'the actual habit tracking is FREE' praised by 13. Report 31: 'supporting a small team' was an E1 purchase trigger ('there is a small team behind so I was happy to pay'; 'happy to support the designers'). Report 33: supporting a small team was a purchase trigger ('I can see this team cares'); 48 call the free tier sufficient (mean 4.85); Vietnamese reviewers take pride in a Vietnamese-built app. Report 34: supporting a solo developer is a named purchase motive ('I paid the app to support solo developer'); 13 of 51 payers praise the developer. Report 36: patronage 5 of 34 payers (14.7%) — 'l'idée de payer 15€ par an pour féliciter, soutenir et remercier le travail d'une équipe indépendante'; proof-first 6 of 34 (17.6%) — 'Have been having it for free until today and decided to purchase'. Report 41: 'Just bought the premium to support the developer i don't even need the features tbh'; decisions made in 20 minutes to a few days on a 3-habit free tier. Report 43: 'I purchased the premium version because I want to support the excellent privacy and pricing policies!'; 'you wouldn't do your job for free. Don't expect programmers to work for free either'; 'I wanna donate the developer'.

title: Weight English-speaking rich markets; volume ≠ revenue
statement: Purchase-signal density is 8.5× higher in the US than China; BR/MX/ES/FR volume is localisation-blocked. Report 16 (contested): the price backlash was STRONGER in high-spend markets — a value-comparison effect ('not worth it at any price', measured against Streaks, Notion, Procreate) — while the rest of the world's complaint was language. Report 20: revocation and delivery grievances were concentrated in the high-spend storefronts (us, gb, de, ca, au, fr: revocation 19.3% vs 8.1% in ru/ua; widget 7×) — the damage landed on the revenue-generating cohort; Russia's higher mean reflected when its users arrived and what they bought, not a better product. Report 23 (counter-evidence): in a paid-up-front app the high-spend and high-volume storefront groups are statistically indistinguishable (4.22 vs 4.22) and only marginally better than the rest of the world (4.12) — what varies by country is which complaint dominates, not how much. Report 24 (counter-evidence): the rich English-language storefronts were the worst — US/UK/CA/AU/NZ/IE (62.87% of the corpus) all above the corpus billing rate and all collapsing to 2.1–2.6 in 2024–26, while Latin America and the Gulf held 4.12–4.59; what varies by country is the funnel, not the product. Report 25 (third corpus in a row): high-spend and high-volume storefront groups are indistinguishable (3.74 vs 3.73) and only marginally above the tail (3.62); monetisation friction is identical (22.5% vs 23.0%) — the paywall objection is global, not a low-income-market phenomenon; what differs is the mix (rich markets praise the price and buy lifetime; the rest hit the launch blocker and billing). Report 26 (the reverse pattern): the high-spend markets (us, gb, de, fr, ca, au = 40.84%) rate lowest (4.489 vs 4.626) and complain most about the paywall (15.3% vs 8.7%; cap 6.2% vs 2.2%) — the free-tier design is costing most where the money is; Russia (19.18%, mean 4.697, 85.3% 5★) and Brazil (4.663) are the happiest markets. Report 27: high-spend markets (92, mean 4.641) and the rest (46, 4.652) are indistinguishable; free-praise appears in 12 of 23 storefronts with no income split — the anti-paywall stance is category-wide. Report 28: the high-spend group (us, cn, jp, gb, de, fr, kr, ca, au, tw = 67.1%) rates lower (3.956 vs 4.181) with ad complaints 5.5pp higher and paywall friction 2.5× higher; GB complains about ads more than the US yet rates higher ('I love this, please fix the ads'); the US carries 71% of payers and the most precise criticism. Report 29 (fourth corpus): high-spend markets rate 0.27 lower and report bugs 3.5× more while praising zero cost at the same rate (48.0% vs 44.0%) — the appeal of free is uniform across income bands; India (mean 4.895, zero bug reports) is not comparable as satisfaction because its reviews are shorter and post-fix, but its dark-mode rate is the strongest country-level feature signal. Report 30 (fifth corpus): the high-spend group (US, GB, FR, DE, JP, KR — 58 reviews) is 67% templated and yields 8 substantive reviews at mean 3.50 vs a 4.79 headline; volume and signal are inversely related — the long tail (36 reviews, 69% substantive) carries the real signal: 47.2% monetisation complaints at mean 3.19. Report 31: high-spend storefronts (78.0%) and the rest of world are almost identical on sentiment (2.34 vs 2.42) but high-spend reports the money story (1.9× cap, 1.4× friction, 1.9× support-unresponsive) and the rest of world the crash wave and language (3.3× localisation); the tail of 71 small storefronts rates better (2.58) than the 9 core ones (2.30) — the more reviewers engaged with paying, the worse the rating. Report 33: high-spend storefronts rate lower (3.60 vs 3.93; ≈3.70 without China) and differ in what money buys — 1.6× payers, 3× Premium not granted, 2.3× billing integrity — with price objection identical (5.2%); the 81-storefront tail rates higher and pays less (3.89 vs 3.71). Report 34: the US (265) is the comparison-shopping market — competitors named 2×, payers 9.06% vs 5.65%, price praise 2× — with less wall friction but 9 of the 14 explicit churn reviews; non-US users hit the cap (6.07% vs 3.77%) and the English-only UI more. Report 36: US 252 (4.095) is the outcome market (outcomes 15.08% vs 6.94%) and reports confusion 3.4× more (onboarding 4.76% vs 1.39%); non-US reviews are feature-request-shaped (unmet 25.69% vs 11.90%) and ask for sync 4× more (9.72% vs 2.38%); the monetisation problem is identical across both. Report 41: high-spend markets self-report paying 2.4× more (9.59% vs 4.00%) and hit the cap 2.3× less; subscription objections are 9 of 10 inside high-spend markets; the UK is the best market (zero cap complaints, 12.5% payers), Canada the most price-sensitive yet most-converting (17.6% objections, 13.7% payers). Report 42: a $39.99–$59.99 app almost absent from high-spend markets (63 of 206; Germany, Australia, China zero) and rated worst there once bursts are removed (2.587); its review base moved to Brazil and Russia, and 20 long-tail storefronts show 46.9% cap complaints with one payer — 'an uncontrolled A/B test of paywall-first onboarding with no trial' (mean 2.906). Report 43: a 64% US corpus where the high-spend group (79.15%) is indistinguishable from the rest (4.006 vs 4.045) and every language request comes from outside it; non-US reviewers self-report paying more (10.04% vs 6.11%, weak) and criticise the dated design more (4.37% vs 1.47%).

title: Free trial before purchase
statement: Weak but present complaint. Report 9: no trial in most storefronts drew 52 explicit requests, several saying they would have bought — and a trial offered in the US but not Saudi Arabia was compared in public. Report 23: a paid-up-front app with no trial — 15 (0.21%, mean 2.40) name the absence, it recurs as a stated regret in refund reviews, and accidental one-tap purchases drive Korea's 6.5% refund rate (7× global); counter-evidence: 'There's no trial because it doesn't need one'. Report 28: five reviewers wanted to pay and were stopped by the absence of a trial — 'I wouldn't have purchased until I was sure I liked the app, and it was impossible to like the app when it was a slew of ads'; 'Unlike Study Bunny, there is no $2.00 30-day trial… that's a full STOP sign'; the dominant purchase trigger is ad removal after sustained free use, which the 'unusable' churners never reach; the sibling app's reported $2 / 30-day trial is the proposed experiment. Report 30: 'I paid the anual subscription… It doesn't have a trial version and it wasn't what I was looking for' (1★); 'before buying something you should be able to try it' (1★); one 3★ could not tell whether the app was paid or free — introduce a trial or a reversible first purchase. Report 31: trial reaction is net-negative (56, mean 2.16) and the positive outcomes are first-year discount trials, not free trials ('an almost-free year is more than enough to know whether the €60 is worth it'). Report 33: for most of the corpus there was no trial ('Three habits, and three days, is simply too little'), and purchase intent 'would buy if…' appears in 44. Report 34: no trial (2022, 2024, 2026) vs a 3-day trial (2025) — 7 complaints (mean 3.00): 'I refuse to pay the min. $9 just to find out if I like it'; a 2018 reviewer proposes '21 days of all bells and whistles … Once you hook them on, charge them'. Report 36: TRIAL 7 (mean 2.43) — 'any sort of trial period — even just an hour — before you blow $15'; 'these issues aren't readily apparent from the free version when you only have two habits to look at'. Report 42: 'no trial' is the lowest-mean theme in the corpus (14, 6.80%, mean 1.29); reviewers name the length they wanted (1 day, 3 days, 7 days, a month) and four met the paywall before any use ('Literally two seconds after downloading'); the report distinguishes it from the cap complaint — a trial asks for temporary full product and is strictly cheaper to grant. Report 43 (counter-case): only 4 of 638 asked for a time-limited trial because a full-featured 3-habit free tier served as one ('The free version has all the features but limits the amount of habits… try it out and if it works for you, you can upgrade as I did') — vs 14 in report 42's 3-habit-plus-paid-basics corpus.

title: Price level — where 'fair' turns into 'too expensive'
statement: Both coexist for one price; split follows market, payment rails and year. Report 20: $39.99/year for a checkbox app was rejected in every market and language for seven years; Spain, which arrived after the conversion and lost nothing, objected to price (16.9%) but not revocation (2.8%) — the grievance follows arrival date, not nationality. Report 23: price objection 123 (1.69%, mean 2.21, 50.4% 1★) with au 5.7%, de 3.8%, ca 3.6% vs us 1.3%; flat across a 2.5× price rise; China's 1★ reviews are almost uniformly '¥25/30 for a reminder'; Germany objected to €3.99 at launch ('99Ct wären OK'). Report 24: price objection 791 (1.82%, mean 2.248) is about magnitude relative to category ($40/quarter, $80–100/month with bundles vs $5–20/yr rivals), opacity and targeting (premium wellness pricing for people with executive dysfunction and low income) — not the existence of a price; a distinct group calls $20/yr worth every penny. Report 25: only ~12 of 55 price objections are about the level ('£25 for a basic box checker'; '$40??? it's a simple app'); ~8 are stated inability to pay (a student, a child); US names the highest figures ($13/mo, $49 lifetime); Argentina (n=40, mean 2.95, friction 40%) is the most hostile storefront. Report 26: price objection 29 (0.76%, mean 2.76) vs 57 defending the price — 2:1 in favour; high-spend markets (de 19.83%, fr 20.37%, au 18.52%, ca 15.60% friction) are where price-defence arguments are also most articulate. Report 28: 16 price objections (1.95%, mean 2.88) at ~$10–15 consumable tiers — 'too expensive for an unproven, ad-saturated experience, sold as an opaque bundle, with no way to try it'; 'not the level of quality that this kind of money gets you with apps like procreate'; students and minors cannot pay ('strict parents and only my mom knows my Apple ID'); the winning position is 'more affordable alternative' to Finch — do not raise the price. Report 30: the price objection (5, mean 1.40) is price ÷ what you get free — 'Es un check list CARÍSIMO'; 'The price is too high for this quality'; 'para ser de pago es demasiado simple' — while three say the price itself is acceptable, two of them rating 1★/2★ for the cap; 'do not cut the price'. Report 31: 'a subscription for a checklist is unjustifiable' ('almost the price of Disney+!'; 'In this economy?'; 'How is this app worth $499.99?') — price objection 379 (7.31%, mean 1.79), 4.1% (E1) → 13.0% (E2); Canada has the highest price objection (11.6%); do not conclude 'lower the price' alone — restore a trustworthy low-commitment path and make it work. Report 33: price objection 203 (5.15%, mean 2.64), highest in Germany (14.7%), Turkey (10.5%) and France (10.4%) — '269 roubles … I pay 400 for Netflix'; '43 euro … for an agenda???'; '€40 … vous vivez où, Monaco?'. Report 34: ~$9/mo, ~$20/yr, ~$40 lifetime — price objection 25 (mean 3.16), many 'great app, too expensive' at 4–5★; €9.99/month called 'completely of the charts'. Report 36: ~$15/£15/€18 a year for Habits alone and ~$30 for the suite (2022–25) rising to $59–70 by 2026; price objection 36 (mean 2.31) and 'not worth it' 21 (mean 2.24, zero 5★). Report 41: lifetime moved €22 (2021) → €28 (2023) → €22–25 / $22.99 (2026) and price objections tracked it (4.2% 2022, 4.6% 2025, 0% 2026); reserve prices named €10, <$5, £3.99. Report 42: $39.99–$59.99/yr (US), ¥6,900 (JP, both reviews 1★), R$79.90 per 12 weeks (BR) vs 500₽ (RU, 'that's nothing'); price objection 18 (mean 1.67, never above 3★) — 'you pay that much for barely any technology'; 'the subscription price is unreal for what the app delivers'. Report 43: at $2.99 the price objection (36, 5.64%, mean 2.31) was almost entirely an objection to being stopped, not to money ('you can easily set timers on your phone for free'; 'I'm a college student so I'm ~broke~'), and it vanished with the cap.

title: Paying customers are the highest 1★ risk — every paid feature must work
statement: Paid cohort rates a full point lower; 28% of payers leave 1–2★; confirmed buyers ×6.7 on 1★. Report 10: paid-cohort mean fell 4.40 → 2.96 across 2022–2026 while the corpus mean barely moved; the five highest paid lifts are all billing mechanics, not price. Report 16: 17 confirmed payers rated 1.21 stars below everyone else; five of the seven billing complaints in the corpus came from them. Report 18: 161 confirmed payers rated 0.30 below the corpus with 21.7% at 1★; their rates of entitlement failure (9.94% vs 1.22%), data loss (12.42% vs 6.01%) and billing dispute (14.29% vs 7.03%) were roughly double the global rates, and by the last era 4.36% of all reviews came from someone who had paid and could not use what they bought. Report 19: 64 of 105 reviewers were confirmed payers and 63 of them left 1★; one third said they could not get their money back and just under one third that they could not stop paying. Report 20: 908 reviewers with payment evidence averaged 1.55 against 3.61 for everyone else — 2.06 stars lower; 76.8% of revocation complaints, 62.1% of widget complaints and 65.5% of support complaints came from the ~22% who paid; the damage was also concentrated in the high-spend storefronts (revocation 19.3% vs 8.1% in ru/ua, broken widget 7×). Report 23 (everyone paid): reviewers who discuss the transaction average 3.52 vs 4.27 for the rest — a dissonance signal; 'I bought this for the Watch and it doesn't work' are the highest-value churn events. Report 24: reviewers who discuss the transaction average 2.006 against 4.356 for the rest. Report 25: explicit payers' mean fell 4.23 → 3.16 → 2.68 across eras (n=13/25/19) while the headline fell 0.27; 14% of payers raise a billing dispute, 8.8% lost access to something bought, 8.8% hit a reliability failure; 52 of 302 one-star reviews (17.2%) show paid evidence — failed customers, not non-buyers venting. Report 26: explicit payers (72) rate a full point below the corpus (3.56 vs 4.570), flat across five years; their top problems are losing the purchase (16.7%) and paywall friction after paying (23.6%). Report 28: identifiable payers rate 3.75 vs 4.03 and 41.7% of them report a failed purchase; a 5★ payer still getting ads writes 'Maybe it just needs to sync up'. Report 30: of the six reviewers who reached payment, five had a bad outcome and none describes a satisfactory purchase; the corpus cannot see quiet happy payers. Report 31: explicit payers went from the happiest segment (E1 mean 3.76) to the angriest (E4 1.35) while their share of reviews rose six-fold to 25.0%; 17.2% of 1★ reviews are from people who say they paid; within 625 payers: not granted 48.6% (1.21), support unresponsive 34.2%, still upsold 31.5%, lag 13.3% ($79.99, freezes on the third habit); a share bought only to make the pop-up go away. Report 33: 427 explicit payers (10.84%, mean 3.16) are polarised — 212 rate 4–5★, 172 rate 1–2★; their mood tracks integrity events, not price (E2 3.77 with a stable lifetime app; 2018 2.83 with 25 purchases not applied; E3 2.78 after Habitify X); after paying: reliability 42.6%, integrity 26.7%, support failure 11.9%, regressions 11.5%; nearly one 1★ in five is a payer. Report 34: payers are satisfied (51, mean 4.63) and E5 is their weakest era (4.23) because every low-rating E5 payer reports a broken paid thing — widget, reminders, lifetime entitlement — not price. Report 36: payers are the least satisfied identifiable group — 34 payers average 3.794 (23.5% 1–2★) vs corpus 4.039 and free-tier praisers 4.88 — because paying exposes no sync (9 of 34, 26.5%), entitlements that don't travel, billing edge cases and bugs ('please fix the bugs (paying user)'). Report 41: 5 of 29 1★ (17.2%) are payers whose specific purchase rationale failed — backfill, Mac sync, Watch sync without iCloud, Health sync, refund; 10 of 60 payers report a post-purchase failure. Report 42: payers (29) rate 2.72 vs non-payers 3.20, 44.8% of them 1★, none 4★ — 'no such thing as a mildly satisfied paying customer'; 9 of 29 hit a defect after paying (freezing '5 minutes to mark two tasks', a launch crash, disappearing habits, premium stats miscalculating). Report 43: payers (48, 7.52%) rate 3.58 vs 4.05 and are 1.9× as likely to give 1★; 11 of 48 (22.9%) hit a defect after paying and 10 of 76 one-star reviews are payers — every one a delivery failure (re-buy after reinstall, restore failed, 'Had it for two minutes after I paid for it and it's glitching', won't open with data gone despite iCloud, a lifetime payer with no support reply, the 2025 popup regression).

title: Focus timer
statement: Meaningful in the US, emerging globally. Report 23: timed tasks and a built-in Pomodoro exist; the Pomodoro break cycle was reported broken in 2022 and timers desync between devices. Report 24: a deep-work ramp-up ritual and per-habit timers are named by long-tenure users as the reason they renew. Report 25: a built-in timer that keeps counting past the goal is praised at mean 4.60 (15, 1.15%). Report 28: a timer with auto-mark-complete exists; three want it to run in the background / on the lock screen. Report 36: a timer / pomodoro requested by 4 (mean 2.50), one because a screenshot habit was named 'Run 15 minutes'. Report 41: a per-habit timer with Live Activities praised by 27. Report 43: multi-step timed routines (morning routines, workouts, kids, ADHD) with background-music fade and voice prompts are a core differentiator and the mechanic the ADHD segment names most.

title: Fitness / health tracking use case
statement: Very strong US use case. Report 31: health and medical routines praised by 36 (hip-surgery physio, Ménière's, a 95-day medication streak); life outcomes 113 (34 kg, 15 lb). Report 33: life outcomes 205 (on the way to 100 books; out of depression; quitting smoking; 1,000+ gym days); medical / mental-health use 20 (mean 4.70).

title: Parents tracking kids
statement: Distinct use case; ties to profiles. Report 23: tracking a child's chores alongside your own is one reason for more capacity (3 reviews). Report 26: one reviewer bought it for an elderly parent and one for their children; ages 10–21 self-identify. Report 31: family/child use praised by a handful — a parent tracking attention to each child; a 5-year-old's morning list.

title: Check-off sound and haptic
statement: Named as a reason to keep coming back. Report 16: the press-and-hold fill with a haptic reward was the product's most-praised craft ('Pavlovian in a good way'; 'I'm beginning to crave that feeling') — praise fell three-quarters after a redesign replaced the circles with a list. Report 31: musical completion sounds and haptics are free and part of the category-winning basics (82 mentions, mean 3.62); 7 find sounds interrupt audio. Report 36: hold-to-check with haptics, sound and music is the most specific praise (57, 10.56%, mean 4.61) — 'a small dose of dopamine every time you check something off' — 'the hardest for a competitor to copy'; 'the music is absolutely gorgeous, please upload it to Spotify'. Report 43: 'paid for the full version because i really like the happy sound when completing tasks'.

title: Use the language users use: Atomic Habits, 75 Hard
statement: Framing seen in US reviews. Report 23: 14 reviews name Atomic Habits (mean 4.79); also Mini Habits, The Power of Habit, Deep Work and The Power of Full Engagement. Report 24: Atomic Habits adjacency is a named purchase trigger.

title: Never ship and walk away
statement: Abandonment is visible to users within a year; the app becomes an OS-release liability for paying users with no recourse, while the store rating quietly rises on survivorship. Report 8: a ~18-month pause let iOS updates break the create flow, widget and launch, and users publicly asked whether the app was abandoned ('Wrapped 2022' still in settings in 2025). Report 14: a solo-developer app broke at each major iOS transition ('Same thing happened with iOS 13 and it took them a while to fix it'), went five years without an update, and the last thing the corpus records is the product and its checkout failing at once. Report 17: a developer who in early 2022 emailed users personally when their feature shipped had gone silent by 2023 — not an absence of ability but its exhaustion; bug reports at each iOS transition then had nobody to fix them. Report 20: across 92 months no significant new capability shipped — the only material changes were the paywall, a widget that never worked and two data-destroying updates; 'ZERO updates, content, features… NOTHING that justifies a yearly subscription fee.' Report 25: a solo developer's fast turnaround (24-hour fixes) thinned across eras (support praise 3.0% → 0.9%) while a launch blocker survived two release cycles. Report 28: 'incentives stop after level three hundred… makes me assume the developers have taken their hands off the wheel'; the listing's last version is ten months stale. Report 31: after a Dec 2020 sale ('sold from Tree Betty to this new owner') the new operator went silent on support and legacy purchases while escalating monetisation — 'ever since the original designer/developer sold it … it's stopped working'.

title: Writes to shared system stores (calendar, health) must be exact and reversible
statement: A paid calendar sync that corrupts the user's calendar is the most severe complaint class in report 2. Report 25: Apple Health values read wrongly — weight interpreted as entry-count, steps off by 568 — in an app whose Health integration is otherwise praised. Report 31: Apple Health counts wrong or doubled in 37 (2.7.1 added a year of steps; sleep 14 h; 26,000 vs 5,000 steps) — de-duplicate imports and show the source value alongside the app's value. Report 33: Health sleep double-counting and data wiped when switching tracking mode — de-duplicate, allow manual override.

title: Manual reordering, renaming and editing of habits/tasks — free
statement: Trivial, requested for years by 5★ users; best effort-to-goodwill ratio. In report 4 rename/reorder was gated and it was the top complaint among paying users. Report 25: habit/group order resets itself (11, 0.84%) — two long-term users left over it; make reordering a drag gesture. Report 26: reorder habits / per-habit gardens / categories requested by 18 (0.47%). Report 27: habit reordering shipped (between Sept 2024 and Aug 2025) and the order does not stick ('they keep getting jumbled up and going back to the wrong spots'); one user avoids reordering for fear of data loss; another wants grouping by the time a habit is set for. Report 29: 'This could be my perfect habit tracker if I could only reorder the list of tasks… Without it the app is virtually useless' (2★); two of four ask to sort by reminder time, which needs no new data model. Report 31: custom order and forced grouping (22) and an edited habit jumping to the top of the list drew complaints — restore custom ordering and stop moving edited habits. Report 33: custom ordering that sticks requested / broken in 47 (90 routines; broken in v10.7.4–10.7.5 and again in 2026). Report 36: cannot delete or rename a habit easily (10, mean 3.00) and a habit-name character limit (3). Report 43: drag-to-reorder within time windows requested by 7 and shipped Nov 2025 ('The ability to program your day windows and reorder items in time windows is fantastic'); bulk edit across a group 1.

title: Customisable, louder reminder sounds
statement: Asked by happy users; the cheapest 5★ upgrade. Report 20: one reminder per habit with user-written message text — 'small feature, outsized affection' (25 reviews, mean 4.60).

title: Skippable, replayable onboarding tour
statement: Hidden gestures (swipe-to-complete, mode toggles) confuse new users; a US-specific 6% complaint in report 2. Report 12: an unskippable narrated intro drew 21 complaints peaking at 16% of 2024 reviews, then fell to one review after a skip control landed — the corpus's clearest fix — while the same intro is praised as a conversion asset. Report 17: a product with its own vocabulary ('what is a sequence? What is a block? What is an activity?') asked for 'a day of experimenting'; users who got through the first day gave 5★, those who didn't quit at 30 minutes — while the paywall demanded payment before that day. Report 18: a five-year vocabulary muddle (습관 vs 루틴 vs 모드) and an onboarding that re-ran on existing and paying accounts with no skip button — a restore-purchase loop returned users to the questionnaire. Report 23: an icon-only first run left new users unable to delete, edit or undo — 63 of 650 1★ reviews; a 66-upvote review asks for plain-language in-app instructions; replace it with a short text-labelled walkthrough covering add / complete / edit / delete / undo / pages. Report 25: confusing/no-guidance 27 (2.06%, mean 2.70); two Brazilian reviewers ask for a tutorial video; comprehension failures worth designing against — how to structure a bad habit ('smoked' or 'didn't smoke'), pinning a weekly habit to a day, stopping a repeat, whether the app is iOS-only. Report 27: a real first-run comprehension cost — four of five confused reviewers got past it and stayed ('a lil hard to figure out at first but now super easy'), the fifth gave 1★; a 30-second skippable explainer is a low-risk fix that does not compromise minimalism. Report 28: 38 onboarding complaints (4.63%, mean 3.24) with one unchanged content for four and a half years — the tutorial teaches the fiction (bunny, mess, carrots) but not how to add, edit or delete a habit ('The tutorial is pointless as they don't show you how to create a task'; 'a steep learning curve with all the unlabeled icons'); 11 more report the add/edit controls genuinely broken and the app cannot tell which it is receiving; the fix is a labelled, skippable tutorial that demonstrates habit CRUD. Report 36: onboarding complaints 16 (mean 1.81, 12 of 16 1–2★), 7.9% of E1 → 1.9% of E5 — 'Is there no manual? Or user guide? I see no way to add new items like a + sign'; 'Is it a game or some kind of something else?' Report 41: onboarding 8 (mean 2.88, lowest non-monetisation) — 'How to use this app🤡 :: Is there a tutorial?'; could not find how to edit a habit; a paying user never started because the skip / miss / stats model was opaque; the report proposes a one-screen 'how this app models habits' card. Report 42: 'Endless screens asking unnecessary questions with no option to skip. I deleted the app after about 15 non-shippable screens, never got to use it'; '~30 questions before I gave up' (both 1★). Report 43: 20 reviews over nine years say there is no tutorial, FAQ or help (see C259).

title: Never seed the launch rating — templated or bought reviews decay and leave the markets they cover unmeasurable
statement: Users spot it in week one and say so; it contaminates the analytics baseline permanently. Report 16: a reviewer alleged the beta list was asked to 'overcome outdated reviews'; 23 self-identified beta testers were strongly bimodal and the launch rating was spent within six weeks. Report 19: all eight 5★ reviews in a 441-day corpus landed in one nine-day December window, all US, 44–74 characters, morning-UTC, generic register, one containing a homoglyph ('recọmmend') — the report treats them as unable to bear analytical weight and states every positive figure with and without them. Report 30: two dated phrase-bank campaigns seeded 50% of all reviews; when they stopped the rating fell toward 3.0★ and the organic 1★ rate tripled. Report 30: 83 of 166 reviews (50%) came from a five-phrase list in several languages, all 5★, in two dated campaigns; when they stopped the half-year mean fell 4.65 → 3.00, the organic 1★ rate rose 12.5% → 44.4%, and the US and GB storefronts were left commercially unmeasured (the high-spend group yielded 8 substantive reviews at 3.50 against a 4.79 headline). Report 43: 13 US 5★ reviews within 24 minutes on 10 Oct 2016 ('Use!!', 'Best!!', 'Helful'), three days after the first review — lifted 2016's mean 4.45 → 4.58 and the ten-year mean by 0.02; detected by timestamp clustering, not votes.

merged_from.title: Never seed the launch rating with templated or bought reviews — the rating decays and the markets they cover become unmeasurable
merged_from.note: C244 (report 30: two phrase-bank 5★ campaigns, 50% of the corpus) is the strongest instance of C076, not a separate rule

title: Purchase and signup flow must not leak buyers
statement: People who try to pay and cannot (errors, rejected emails, promos that fail to apply) leave 2–4★ and money on the table. Report 14: two willing buyers in 2020 could not complete the purchase ('When I click upgrade button, it only appears an orange screen and then disappears') — the checkout broke in the app's final months.

title: Ship the paid feature working before you sell it — the purchase trigger must never be the broken feature
statement: Paid features carry a higher reliability bar; selling broken sync/calendar/stats put payers a full star below free users. Report 20: the widget was by a wide margin the most-named purchase trigger and the feature that most often didn't work — 182 reviews (mean 1.94), 113 from confirmed payers, broken for five years with an in-app FAQ offering 'restart your phone'; even when present it was a Today-view widget while screenshots implied Home Screen. Ship it properly or remove it from the paywall copy and refund on request. Report 23: the Apple Watch is a purchase driver, not a feature — ≥15 reviews name it as the reason to buy and the explicit-bug subset runs at mean 2.57; if you ship a Watch app its reliability budget is your main reliability budget. Report 41: four of ten post-purchase failures bought for one named capability that then failed (backfill, widget ×2, Health sync) — any single-feature failure is a total failure of the purchase. Report 43: 'purchase not delivered' is the most damaging pattern for a one-time product — 4 buyers got nothing ('I paid to upgrade to get the edit function, but no changes happened… Something broken in the backend??'; 'Purchase premium but still getting free trial capabilities'; 'just took my money'), one could not buy, one could not restore.

merged_from.title: Never take a paying user's reason to buy away — the widget sold the upgrade and never worked
merged_from.note: C220 (report 20's widget: the #1 named purchase trigger, non-functional for five years) is the strongest instance of C078, not a separate rule

title: Personal photos as habit icons
statement: Rare, loved, and no competitor in report 2's corpus offers it.

title: Colour themes / dark mode
statement: 'Only green' draws requests; cheap. Report 10: dark mode requested since 2022 as an accessibility need (migraine, light sensitivity). Report 20: dark mode moved from free-ish to paid in the 2021 conversion (89 reviews, mean 2.69) and was a named purchase trigger. Report 24: dark mode requested by 43, 58.1% of them 4–5★ — cheap and asked for by advocates. Report 29: dark mode absent — 15 requests (4.10%, mean 4.67, the highest-satisfaction request group), India 8.77% (2.9× global), 'it's what's missing for 5 stars'. Report 31: dark mode / themes 18; a German visually impaired reviewer: 'no accessibility features, no dark mode, no localisation … unusable'. Report 33: dark mode and themes were Premium in 2019–20; 48 request themes / colours. Report 43: per-habit colours / icons requested by 4 (mean 4.50); dark mode praised.

title: Ads in the free tier
statement: A mild negative and a minor purchase reason in report 2; 'no ads' is the best-rated topic in report 1. Report 18: an interstitial ad on every check-off (Oct 2022) drew 17+ protests in weeks and was softened by December; the surviving minimal ads were tolerated. Report 25: six reviewers volunteer 'show me ads instead' of a paywall — ads-as-alternative is requested, not complained about; the app has none. Report 26: three teens independently ask for a rewarded-ad path to extra habits ('I will watch ads all day long if I have to') while 7 reviews (mean 5.00) praise having no ads. Report 27: 12 reviews (8.70%, mean 4.83) praise the absence of ads by name; an ad tier is 'contradicted by evidence'. Report 28 (the strongest counter-evidence in the set): an ad-supported free tier whose interstitial fires on every check-off is 19.98% of reviews at mean 2.73 vs 4.35 for the rest, 52.4% of all 1★, and rose from 3.5% (2021H2) to 39.6% (2024H2) before easing to 16.7%; three reports of non-dismissible ads and one of 'decline the rewarded ad, get a forced ad anyway' are store-guideline risks; an app rated 4+ with 40 reviews from or about children (ages 8–10 self-declared) serves untargeted network ads including AI homework-cheating and Temu wigs; 6 reviewers praise the ads as light and rewarded ads for carrots are accepted — the placement, not the existence, is the damage; the CN storefront (12 reviews, zero ad complaints) may be a natural ad-free control. Report 42: zero mentions of ads; upsell interstitials play the role ('the popups for premium are annoying and difficult to click out of'); one would rather see ads than pay €1.99/month (report 34).

title: Performance must not degrade with habit count
statement: 5+ second taps for the most engaged (paying) users; lag is a churn cause on its own. Report 30: above ~10 habits the list jumps back to the top after every tick and rows cannot be made denser — a defect that only paying users hit; fix it before raising the cap. Report 31: freeze / lag 404 (7.79%, mean 1.62) rising in every era to 26.6% of 2025–26 — '10 seconds for the sound effect, another 20 seconds for the colour to change'; '20-30 seconds per habit'; 'it now takes several seconds to add a single entry … can't cope with too many entries' (iPhone 15 Pro) — set a tap-to-register budget (<100 ms) and test with multi-year histories; some reviewers infer throttling of non-subscribers (untested). Report 42: lag scales with habit count ('the more goals you add the slower it gets'; hit at 15 habits) — 12 reviews (mean 2.58), 9 Brazilian, 4 payers — 'the users most affected are the ones who bought the app to have more than three habits'.

title: Address tracking / privacy visibly
statement: One unrebutted 1★: 'a whole lotta tracking going on by the developer'. Report 13: a 2017 privacy-policy revision drew 11 reviews in a month; location prompts with no stated purpose ('No, you don't need it') and disclosure-to-law-enforcement language made long-time users delete. Report 24: privacy / personal data complaints 138 (mean 1.225, 87.7% 1★) — a long questionnaire and web billing that collects card data before install. Report 27: a no-data-collection privacy label and no account are praised as features (4, mean 5.00); data monetisation is contradicted by the evidence and the listing. Report 29: 'I also appreciate that there's no subscription fees or ads. Am I trading off data privacy for this?' — users of free apps look for the hidden price; the listing's privacy label did not obviously cover the bandwidth-sharing prompt that followed. Report 34: on-device data with no account praised as privacy (7): 'my data isn't stored on a server!'; 'hasn't been larded with privacy-invading trackers'. Report 36: 'Does what it's meant to do while respecting your privacy and not harvesting your data'; 'the developers don't collect your data'. Report 41: 'This app doesn't hoard your data'; privacy / no account 10 reviews, all 5★. Report 43: 'Great data privacy (no data collected)' is enumerated among purchase reasons; 'I want to support the excellent privacy and pricing policies!'

title: Never imply cross-app integration you don't have
statement: Sibling apps raised expectations of integration; the purchases it drove ended in 1★.

title: No rating-prompt or cross-promo spam, especially to payers
statement: Small but consistent complaint.

title: Promos, giveaways and gift codes must work exactly as advertised
statement: Inflate early sentiment; when the promo fails to apply it produces 2–3★ from would-be buyers. Report 5's '1+1' gift code could not be used by the buyer and expired in three months — six years of disputes. Report 9: an advertised 3-month money-back guarantee was not honoured (17 reviews); withdrawing the claim zeroed those complaints and halved refund complaints. Report 26: China App Store shows a ¥38 tier with no in-app purchase path. Report 31: '83–90% off' first-year offers ($8.99–$9.99) checked out at $59.99–$99.99 through 2022–23, and a $19.99 'lifetime' was shown against anchors of $399–CA$499.99 that charged without unlocking. Report 34: the ~29 Jun 2023 free-lifetime giveaway left one reviewer calling it a 'Scam of free life time subscription' (1★) and another asking when the next limited-time free offer comes. Report 42: a promotional R$39.90/year shown, R$99.90 charged at confirm (1★, 'I'm waiting to adjust my rating of the app'). Report 43: a promo-free, ad-free one-time model produced zero unexpected charges, trial traps or chargebacks in 638 reviews.

title: Destructive actions on widgets, quick surfaces and running routines need confirmation or undo
statement: An un-undoable reset button on a Home Screen widget destroyed streaks by mis-tap and read as 'a visual cue to break the streak' — a safety issue in a recovery app.

title: Regional pricing
statement: IN, TR, UA, BR, MX, SA reviewers name price as the only blocker; India likes the product and has not yet been asked a price it can accept. Report 23: price objection concentrates in au (5.7%), de (3.8%), ca (3.6%) against us 1.3%; China's number is ¥25–30. Report 25: price-display confusion is a Mexico-specific repeated issue — three reviewers cannot tell pesos from dollars, others name MXN 500, 40, 300, 599 and 299.99 — a pricing-display problem that is cheap to fix; Argentina's hostility (mean 2.95) warrants a look at its pricing display and trial mechanics. Report 33: regional price objections from Vietnam, Turkey (270 TL), Korea ('I'll buy if it's discounted') and Japan (¥19,000 lifetime, 'unfair to base your pricing on [exchange rates] alone'; 「前に比べて値段が爆上がり」) — regionalise lifetime pricing. Report 36: regional pricing complaints from Turkey and a cheaper local rival in India (₹499/yr vs Dayrise). Report 41: purchasing-power-adjusted lifetime tiers proposed for the 63 sub-50 storefronts, where cap complaints are 2.1× the high-volume markets.

title: No upsell nagging without a 'never ask again' option
statement: Full-screen interstitials, permanent banners and upsells before first value draw complaints even from 5★ users; a subscription launch with nagging cost ~3 points of 1–2★. Report 9: upsell-pressure complaints quintupled (2.16% → 4.84% → 10.23%) as the funnel was tuned harder, becoming the fastest-growing 1★ source. Report 14: the cleanest before/after in the set — rating-and-upsell pop-ups on every launch drew six star-docking reviews in nine weeks ('I docked one star for this'; 'Deleted'), and removing them produced unsolicited 5★ praise ('They removed the pop ups. Nice!!') and a named edge over a rival still 'begging for an upgrade within the first minute'. Report 18: a persistent bottom promo bar and a Dynamic Island discount countdown in 2025–26 were experienced as worse than the 2022 interstitial ads ('Absolutely the worst choice'); upgrade-nag was among the lowest-rated themes (40, mean 2.40★). Report 20: a 'limited time offer' countdown that reset to 60 hours on expiry ran for over four years (Jan 2021 → Mar 2025) beside a full-screen launch interstitial with a low-contrast dismiss — 225 reviews (5.56%, mean 1.80); 'Dark patterns make bad UX!'; 'first the consumer must see the value of the product. And what do you have? Every 2 seconds a subscribe banner.' Report 23: 4 reviews object to ads for the developer's other apps inside a paid app. Report 24: sister-app upsells (308, mean 1.932), referral/share prompts (131) and pop-ups/unskippable steps (182, mean 2.082) inside a paid subscription. Report 25: navigation-blocking upsell sheets — '10 popups in 20 seconds which kills the use'; 'not even my first second on the app 4 ads asking for payment'; a 5-second forced delay on the premium prompt; 'a habit app that starts right away with dark patterns' — 35 reviews (2.67%, mean 1.80); cap the prompt to one dismissible surface per session; a French reviewer notes explosive pop-ups are actively harmful for ADHD users in an app marketed to them. Report 28: forced interstitials on every action ('Ad while you write a habit. Ad while you review habits. Ad while you breathe.') and a rating prompt on open and check-off. Report 31: upsell nag 676 (13.04%, mean 1.72) rising 1.9% (E1) → 22.6% (E4) through a full-screen offer on every launch (2021), a permanent 'Just for you' list cell (2023) and two pop-ups per launch (2024, mean 1.47) — 'the only habit I'm developing is closing the upsell pop up'; a share of E4 purchases were made 'to get rid of the incessant pestering', and when relief did not arrive they produced the angriest reviews; E1 buyers valued 'that they don't prompt you to update every 3 clicks'; cap offers at one dismissible surface per week. Report 34: upgrade nagging 4 (mean 2.00) — 'constantly being nagged to upgrade to premium. I only track one thing'. Report 36: a full-page subscribe screen on every launch — POPUP 24 (mean 2.67), rising to 15.0% of 2026 H2, the only negative theme regularly in 5★ (4 of 24): 'i said no already, please respect that'; 'Can't use the app on my iPhone 13 mini because of a freaking pop up' (5★ titled 'Unusable'); the report calls a once-a-week cap the cheapest change available. Report 42: upsell interstitials 'annoying and difficult to click out of' (3, mean 1.67). Report 43 (counter-case): the in-app upsell is never complained about; the nag is the review prompt.

title: Ask for reviews well — tone converts; cadence and ignoring the OS opt-out backfire
statement: A charming review request produced dozens of reviews; frequent prompts that ignore the iOS opt-out, especially to payers, read as 'scammy'. Cross-promoting the developer's other apps inside the product draws the same complaint (report 2). Cross-promoting the developer's other apps inside the product draws the same complaint (report 2). Report 14: at least three reviews existed only because the app demanded one ('Happy now??'; a body reading 'Review'), polluting the ratings data. Report 20: a review prompt whose decline button read 'let the developers be sad' — 26 reviewers say it is why they wrote (inflating 2019's 5★ count) and two docked stars for the manipulation. Report 23: review-prompt nagging 25 (0.34%, mean 2.72, 40% 1★). Report 24: an in-app review prompt on day 1–3 makes the 5★ band (57.89%, median 105 characters) a first-impression measure — 'they asked me to review it now which I find kind of ridiculous'; the highest-voted reviews are all pre-2024 5★s. Report 25: an onboarding review prompt — 'Why won't it progress without me writing a review?'; 'in the middle of the onboarding questions the app interrupts me to ask me to rate' — pushed ≤25-character reviews from 7.2% to 33.4% of the corpus (150 of 196 5★ in 2026) and median body length from 156 to 53 characters; the all-records mean falls 0.27 while the substantive mean falls 0.73, and 1★ share (16.1% → 26.6%) is the only trustworthy trend line; 43 reviews (mean 4.21) are from people who say they have not used the app yet. A prompt at first launch buys a store rating and costs your own telemetry. Report 26: the app rewards a review with a cosmetic unlock and 13 reviewers say so ('I'm just doing this to get the backgrounds 😋 I haven't even used the app at all'; '(I'm NOT a bot btw)'); ≤25-character reviews rose from 16.5% to 35.0% of the corpus, 83–91% of them 5★; true inflation is unmeasurable and there is App Store policy exposure. Report 27: exactly one reviewer discloses a prompt ('Saw the message and had to rate'), no reward-for-review, and only 12 of 138 reviews are ≤25 characters — the substantive mean (4.594) equals the headline (4.645); a corpus of people who wrote something. Report 28: a rating prompt on open and on check-off shipped in 2026 (5 of 7 complaints are 2026) and already produced a 1★ 'until the rate me notification spam gets fixed'; 134 contentless 5★ records (median 38 chars) suggest the 2026 rating recovery is partly solicited; 'prompting into an ad-frustrated session is actively harvesting negative ratings'. Report 29: a rating prompt fired on the first check-off ('Used the app for 2 minutes then a reminder popped up for me to rate the app. -1 star'; 'so here I am, on day 1') — 39 contentless reviews, all 5★, median 27 characters; the 4.552 mean is partly a prompt-timing artefact that also starves the developer of diagnostic feedback; delay it to day 7 or ~10 completions. Report 30: 83 templated 5★ reviews and a near-absence of 2–3★ (7 of 166) consistent with a prompt routing satisfied users to the store; the public 4.4★ is a decaying artefact. Report 31: no review-prompt inflation — 20 prompt complaints (0.39%) and short reviews ≤7.7% of every era; about 1–2% of 5★ are complaints rated 5 'so people see it'. Report 33: in-app rating prompts 'three in 10 seconds' (Nov 2017 – Jan 2018) made review-nag complaints 3.8% of 2017 before falling to ≤1% every later year; 82 of 88 rating-contradicts-text reviews are 5★ reporting a bug or block; 820 short reviews (20.8%) inflate the positive side. Report 34: a rating prompt during setup ('you want me to rate it before I even finish setting it up'; 'App asks for 5 stars review'); the report recommends prompting after setup and after a 7-day streak. Report 41: 'it asks for a review every day which is needlessly annoying even if you've rated the app' (1★, Aug 2026); 111 of 815 (13.6%) contentless praise at a 69-character median — the signature of prompted reviews. Report 42: a rating prompt inside onboarding — 'Asking for a rating the first time I log in? How could I possibly know. But, since I'm being asked I must give it a one star' — the clearest causal chain to a 1★ in the corpus (2, both 1★). Report 43: the review prompt fires 'every time I open this app', 'every 2 minutes', and to people who already paid ('Paid $3, still kept asking for review. Annoying!') — 4 reviews, mean 2.75, plus a prompt whose Submit stays greyed out; 'a rating-acquisition mechanism actively lowering the rating'.

merged_from.title: No rating-prompt or cross-promo spam, especially to payers
merged_from.note: rating-prompt spam to payers was already the negative half of C094; cross-promo spam folded in

title: Neutral, non-judgemental tone on failure
statement: Reset without shame, no motivational pop-ups, keep history — the differentiation against apps that 'talk'. Report 23: a reminder framed as loss — 'You will lose your streak of X days if you don't do this today' — drew requests in four languages to reframe positively ('pedagogy from the early 20th century'); one string change per locale. Report 24: childish / condescending tone 304 (0.70%, mean 2.701); what paying users value includes that missing a day is not punished. Report 25: 'I clicked, paid £29.99 and I don't even know why. It's a list of aims for the day, I get to see all the things I haven't done and feel bad' — a checklist without a forgiving frame reads as guilt. Report 26: 'accountability and motivation without the shame' — gentleness, no streaks and a calm garden metaphor are the moat (25, mean 4.76; mental-health users 32, mean 4.66). Report 33: guilt copy backfires — 'Let's do better tomorrow, shall we?'; 'Yikes'; a Jan 2026 'Are you sure the day is over?' pop-up on fail/skip with no off switch ('infantilizing … Shipping annoying stuff without an off switch is a churn risk') — 43 reviews on unwanted or guilt notifications (mean 2.33). Report 36: 'As an easily discouraged perfectionist, I LOVE that if you miss a day (or a week) that it doesn't become the app of shame' (20 votes); the motivational text is 'encouraging but never guilt inducing' (13, all 5★).

title: Privacy and discretion stack
statement: Face ID / passcode lock, no account, discreet app name, alternate icons — zero negative reviews in report 3 and category-critical for recovery users on family phones. Report 33: privacy 23 reviews (mean 1.35) — the in-app help showed other customers' support conversations, e-mails and photos; goal-share URLs readable without login with no off switch; sync requiring Apple ID, Google account and e-mail; third-party analytics — audit support-conversation scoping and make sharing opt-in with unguessable, expiring links.

title: A tip / donate option
statement: People asking to give money with no mechanism to do so. Report 8: in a completely free app, 7 users asked unprompted for a tip jar (all 5★) and 13 more volunteered to pay — mostly one-time, not subscription. Report 27: exactly two reviewers volunteer money unprompted — 'Keep the free app, consider adding a tip jar for users who are thankful'; 'it would be nice to donate to the dev since it's a free app' — both 5★, both framing payment as gratitude, both pairing it with staying free; with 10 developer-gratitude reviews (all 5★) a tip jar is the only monetisation the corpus positively endorses, and Canada is where the evidence says to start. Report 29: 'love to be able to contribute to use it' — a contribution offered in a free app, alongside a lifetime-purchase offer tied to a widget.

title: Time-unit flexibility for counters (hours → years)
statement: What makes day 1 survivable for a quit-habit user; zero 1–2★.

title: Countdown / 'days until' mode
statement: Users want one app for count-up and count-down. Report 23: an end-date / countdown / long-term goal is requested by very happy users (17, 0.23%, mean 4.76, 0% 1★).

title: Money-saved counter
statement: Standard in quit-smoking apps; named as the one thing missing.

title: Milestones, achievements, celebration
statement: The largest positive-intent request in report 3 (2.21%, six years); shipped Aug 2026. Report 23: the gold-theme completion state — the whole screen turns gold when every task is done — is named by 80 5★ reviews; rewards, badges and milestones requested 136 times by happy users. Report 31: celebration on completion requested by 44 (mean 3.98), while achievements/trophies added in Apr 2023 were unwanted by long-time users.

title: Inverse / 'good habit' mode for a counter
statement: Recovery users want the number up; chore/ADHD users want it low — one counter, two mental models.

title: Vulnerable users — recovery, mental-health and minors — are a sensitive surface
statement: Alcohol, nicotine, self-harm (incl. minors), drugs, EDs, no-contact; monetisation moves land as 'preying on the vulnerable'; age rating is load-bearing. In report 4: 455 kid/teen reviews who cannot pay, and 89 shame / diet-framing reviews in a 4+ app. Report 24: a product marketed to people with executive dysfunction and low income priced as a premium wellness subscription; diet-culture / eating-disorder trigger complaints (61, mean 2.918); depression/anxiety users are 2.89% of the corpus. Report 26: users describing severe depression, being bedbound, three years clean and wartime anxiety ('This app helped me return to life') — the gentle, non-punitive frame is what serves them; children as young as 10 review the app. Report 28: an app rated 4+ with 40 reviews (4.87%) from or about children — 'I'm ten'; 'im nine'; 'I am a 8 years old' — serves untargeted network ads (AI homework-cheating apps, Temu wigs) and a 'watch an ad to double carrots' prompt; a brand and compliance exposure independent of the rating damage. Report 29: 'You're doing a great service to students who cannot afford to spend on applications' — free access matters to students; 4 student/budget reviews at mean 5.00. Report 31: sobriety, medication and mood-disorder trackers were hit by streak resets, removed quit-to-zero goals and upsells interrupting tracking.

title: Never ship a paywall or feature-removal change silently
statement: Undisclosed changes and 'it was a bug' replies that don't match what users see destroy trust for a year. Report 11: the store description still discloses no paywall at all (0 mentions of premium/subscription/free/unlock) after the retrofit; a grandfathering rule for pre-2026 users is the recommended fix. Report 20: the Feb 2021 restoration was never announced — '4 stars after premium was restored, but not 5 because the devs ignored us for so long and have not acknowledged the issue' — and the March 2025 wipe drew 'no communication whatever about this disaster.' Report 29: the bandwidth-sharing prompt arrived with no announcement; the report's first fix is 'decide and publicly disclose the web-indexing policy'. Report 30: the 2 → 3 cap change shipped without the listing being updated. Report 31: monthly/yearly frequency, streak display, swipe, quit-to-zero, Shortcuts, the tappable widget, 'last done' and day-start time were removed across v2 (Mar 2022) and v3.0 (27 Jan 2023) — feature removal 9.4% of E4, an update blamed for a regression 8.4%; the legacy Premium stopped being recognised in Apr 2023 with no notice. Report 33: Habitify X (~27 Aug 2020) removed time logs, yearly stats, CSV export, swipe, 'N per week', Shortcuts and the Watch app with 'no migration path' — 149 reviews in nine weeks, 42 UPDATE-. Report 36: the Oct 2023 widget gate was read as a bug for months ('the widget app has not been working properly … says that I have to unlock it') and the 2026 cap as 'extremely bugged. I cannot add a second habit'. Report 43: 'pause a habit' vanished in the 2026 update (2★) and 'every 2/3 weeks' schedules silently became weekly after the redesign (4★).

title: Widget variants and customisation as the paid layer
statement: Base single-counter widget free forever; multi-counter widgets, custom art, progress rings, reset-from-widget can be paid — and were report 3's #1 purchase trigger. Report 30 (counter-evidence): a paid widget in a capped tracker lost a user to a competitor with a free widget and is the only named paid feature besides more habits; the report proposes testing widget free vs paid as an acquisition driver. Report 36: once widgets were paid, widget-improvement demand peaked (titles, colours, streak display, interactivity) — 'now that widgets cost money, people want them to do more'. Report 41: widgets are icon-only — 'When you have +10 habits, one habit widget with only icon and no clue to remembering the habit is a pain'; one runs a competitor alongside for text labels (8 requests); widget icons 'Make them bigger and it is 5 stars!'. Report 43: per-habit notification sounds are 'too few' — 'hearing the same sound for every habit… mentally makes me mush all my tasks together'; 'you can't use the notification or ringtone sounds from your iPhone'; a snooze wanted (16, mean 3.94).

title: Goals / targets
statement: Tolerated behind the paywall (mean 4.05) and a stated purchase reason. Report 25: a layer of long-term goals sitting above habits is requested by very satisfied users (7, mean 4.71). Report 41: yearly / long-horizon goals requested by 6.

title: A free trial must be a real trial
statement: It must apply to whichever plan the user picks, and the confirmation must show the exact charge date and amount; a trial that bills at once produced 789 reviews at mean 1.35 in report 4 and must be verified per storefront (Brazil ran 7–11× the global rate). Report 10: 149 users believe they were charged at trial START (mean 1.79) and trial length varied between 2 and 7 days across users. Report 12: a 3-day trial introduced around 2024 shows as subscribed but 'doesn't move past the subscription screen' — the complaint changed shape from 'there is no trial' to 'the trial doesn't work'. Report 13: a trial that cannot start without first authorising a subscription, defaulting to the most expensive annual tier, produced 1,102 auto-charge reviews at mean 1.20 (999 one-star) — the single most damaging mechanic in a 19,850-review corpus; involuntary-charge reviews equalled voluntary-purchase reviews 1:1. Report 18: trials that converted immediately ('in my case there was no free period'; asked for monthly, charged annual; frozen since minute 10, charged a full year) in KR, JP, TW, ID, BR and DE; trial length shrank from 3 weeks to 7 days to 2–3-day variants.
